newsitem.title: USA: Texas Instruments posts loss, stock soars.
newsitem.headline: Texas Instruments posts loss, stock soars.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc. reported a fourth-quarter loss Thursday, but its stock soared nearly 12 percent as investors looked beyond the bottom line and saw a firm recovery in its core semiconductor business.
The Dallas-based company also announced it was selling its unprofitable notebook computer business to Taiwan-based Acer Inc. in order to focus on higher-margin chip markets.

While the terms of the deal were not disclosed, investors welcomed the move and the company's stock jumped $7.50 to a 52-week high of $71 on the New York Stock Exchange, making it one of the biggest and most active shares on the exchange.
Texas Instruments posted a loss of $29 million, or 15 cents per share, in the three months ended Dec. 31, compared with a profit of $291 million, or $1.50 per share, in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Revenues fell to $2.46 billion from $3.15 billion, primarily because of a huge drop in the price of computer memory chips.

But company executives said the results were depressed by one-time charges and that operating profits, excluding those charges, were 67 cents a share, roughly in line with analyst expectations and more than double those of the third quarter.
"The picture on the recovery side is positive," said Jonathan Joseph, an analyst with Montgomery Securities. "The trends are very positive."

Texas Instruments earlier this month sold its defense electronics unit to Raytheon Co. for $2.95 billion, and the sale of the notebook computer unit fit in with the company's plan to focus its efforts on higher-margin digital signal processing solutions, or DSPS, which convert sights and sounds into digital computer language.

"We are accelerating our strategic direction by focusing on businesses, products and technologies that add value for TI and our customers through sustainable differentiation, with high-growth opportunities and improved financial stability," Chief Executive Officer Tom Engibous said. "1997 will be a year of transition."

The notebook computer unit had grown sharply and last year had revenues estimated at $700 million but it was not profitable, and company executives said it would do better as part of a company "with a more complete line of computer products." Texas Instruments and Acer have had a close relationship for many years.
Analysts said the rapid shift away from low-growth businesses to DSPS was transforming Texas Instruments' profile and would boost profits.

"They are becoming an entirely different company. You are not going to recognize them at all in '97," said Daniel Niles, an analyst with Robertson Stephens. "They are blowing out of the unprofitable PC business and are left with the high-growth semiconductor business."

Digital signal processors have over the last 12 months displaced memory chips as Texas Instruments' largest single source of revenues and accounted for about 40 percent of $8.1 billion in total semiconductor revenues last year.
Niles said he expected the company's stock price to double over the next 12 to 18 months.

Chief Financial Officer Bill Aylesworth said the troubled market for memory chips would remain volatile in the short term because of excess supply but that new chip products were taking up much of the slack.
Memory chip prices fell about 80 percent last year and dragged down Texas Instrument's yearly net profits to $63 million, or 33 cents a share, from $1.09 billion, or $5.63 a share, in 1995.

Orders for digital signal processors, however, were 30 percent higher in the fourth quarter, and Aylesworth predicted strong growth in 1997. "We see every indication that the trend of strong revenue growth is going to continue."
